name: AsyncAPI
vendor: AsyncAPI Initiative (Linux Foundation), started by Fran Méndez

foundation.via: A series of LF Projects, LLC

summary: A specification, and a set of open-source tools, for describing event-driven APIs in one YAML or JSON document: the brokers an application connects to, the channels it sends to or receives from, and the messages on them.
intro: AsyncAPI does for message-driven systems what OpenAPI does for HTTP APIs. An AsyncAPI document describes one application: `servers` gives the brokers it connects to and their protocol, `channels` lists the topics or queues it uses (each with an `address` and the `messages` that may appear on it), and `operations` says what the application does on each channel, with an `action` of `send` or `receive`. Payloads are described with AsyncAPI’s Schema Object, a superset of JSON Schema Draft 07, or in another format such as Avro or Protocol Buffers, which tools are recommended but not required to support, and shared schemas, messages and security schemes live under `components`. The current version, 3.1.0, came out on January 31, 2026.

The same format covers many transports. Bindings add protocol-specific details, such as a Kafka topic’s partitions or the QoS level of an MQTT publish, to servers, channels, operations and messages; the specification defines binding keys for 20 protocols, including Kafka, MQTT, AMQP, NATS, Pulsar, Google Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS and SQS, WebSockets and ROS 2. The initiative also maintains the tools that read the format: the AsyncAPI CLI, which validates documents and generates docs or code from templates, Studio for editing documents visually, Modelina for generating payload models in languages such as Java, TypeScript and Go, and parsers for JavaScript and Go.
strengths: One machine-readable contract for an event-driven service, from which docs, payload models and code are generated, the way OpenAPI works for HTTP
Protocol-neutral: the same structure describes Kafka, MQTT, AMQP, NATS, WebSocket and other APIs, with bindings for each protocol’s own settings
Payload schemas are a superset of JSON Schema, and a message may instead point to an OpenAPI, Avro, RAML or Protocol Buffers schema, so existing payload definitions can be reused
Vendor-neutral under the Linux Foundation, with the specification and core tools under Apache 2.0 and no contributor licence agreement for the tools
limits: Version 3.0 changed the core structure: `publish` and `subscribe` became operations with `send` or `receive`, and channel keys became IDs with a separate `address`, so 2.x documents and tools need converting
It describes what an application sends and receives, not how messages flow across a whole system; tracing producers to consumers means relating many documents
Binding support varies by protocol and tool: a binding defined in the specification may be ignored by the generator template or docs renderer you use
A hand-written document drifts from the code unless it is generated from the code or checked in CI

sections.title: What changed between 2.x and 3.0
sections.intro: Version 3.0.0, released on December 5, 2023, is the one major break so far; 3.1.0 only added ROS 2 bindings.

rows.label: Operations
values: A separate `operations` section, each with `action: send` or `action: receive` and a reference to a channel

rows.label: Point of view
values: `publish` meant others could publish to the channel because your application subscribed to it
The document describes what your own application does, so `send` means it sends

rows.label: Channels
values: The channel’s key was also its address, and a channel could not be reused
The key is an arbitrary ID, the address is a separate field, and channels can be reused across documents

story: OpenAPI gave HTTP APIs a shared description format, but systems built on message brokers had nothing similar: teams documented Kafka topics, MQTT topics and AMQP queues by hand. Fran Méndez created AsyncAPI in 2016 to describe such message-driven APIs; it started as an adaptation of the OpenAPI specification, kept as compatible with it as possible so users could reuse parts in both. Version 2.0.0 came out on September 11, 2019.

As adoption grew the project needed a neutral home. On March 30, 2021 the Linux Foundation announced it would host the AsyncAPI Initiative, with Ably, Apideck, Bump, IQVIA, MuleSoft, Slack, Solace and TIBCO as founding sponsors; the release named Adidas, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP and Slack as production users and said production use had tripled from 2019 to 2020. The charter limits how many representatives one company may have on the Technical Steering Committee.

Version 3.0.0, released on December 5, 2023, rebuilt the core around separate operations with a `send` or `receive` action, ending a long-standing confusion over what `publish` and `subscribe` meant. Version 3.1.0 followed on January 31, 2026 with bindings for ROS 2, the robotics middleware.

choices.why: AsyncAPI began as an adaptation of OpenAPI and aimed to stay as compatible with it as possible, so users could reuse parts, such as payload schemas, in both.

choices.choice: Protocol bindings instead of one protocol
choices.why: Event-driven systems run on many brokers, so the core describes channels and messages generically and bindings carry each protocol’s own settings.

choices.choice: Describe the application’s own actions in 3.0
choices.why: In 2.x, `publish` described what other applications could do, which readers kept misreading; `send` and `receive` describe the application itself.

timeline.text: Fran Méndez starts AsyncAPI; the specification repository is created in November
The Linux Foundation announces it will host AsyncAPI, on March 30
AsyncAPI 3.0.0 released on December 5, with operations and send/receive
AsyncAPI 3.1.0 released on January 31, adding ROS 2 bindings
